lead: A closed section, a wing box or a fuselage shell, has no free edge, so the shear flow has nowhere obvious to start. The method is to cut the loop once in imagination, find the open-section flow q<sub>b</sub>, and add a constant flow q₀ round the loop. For a load through the shear centre q₀ is fixed by the condition that the section does not twist. This chapter works the method on a rectangular box, then thickens one wall and shows how the shear centre moves towards it.
prereq: You need: the open-section shear flow from the chapter on open sections; the twist-rate formula used here is derived in the Bredt–Batho chapter.

sections.h3: The cut and the constant q₀

blocks.text: Make an imaginary cut in one wall. The section is now open, and the open-section integral gives a basic flow q<sub>b</sub>, zero at the cut. The real section has no cut, so the real flow is q<sub>b</sub> plus a constant q₀ that runs all the way round and represents the flow at the cut. q₀ is not found from force equilibrium: any constant flow round a closed loop has zero resultant force, only a moment 2Aq₀.

blocks.where: q<sub>s</sub> is the actual shear flow (N/mm); q<sub>b</sub> is the open-section flow from the cut (N/mm); q<sub>s,0</sub> is the constant flow at the cut (N/mm), positive in the same direction as s.

blocks.text: Two conditions can fix q₀. If the load position is known, take moments of q about any point and equate them to the moment of the load. If the shear centre is wanted, impose zero twist instead. The rate of twist of a closed cell is (1/2AG)∮q ds/t, so zero twist means:

blocks.where: t is the wall thickness (mm); ds is a length of mid-line (mm); the integrals go once round the loop in the direction of s. With uniform t, q<sub>s,0</sub> = −(1/L)∮q<sub>b</sub> ds, L being the perimeter.

items: Find the centroid and I<sub>xx</sub> (and I<sub>yy</sub>, I<sub>xy</sub> if the section is unsymmetric), using mid-line dimensions.
Choose the cut. A cut on an axis of symmetry is convenient, but any cut gives the same final q.
Integrate q<sub>b</sub> = −(S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub>)∫t y ds from the cut, y being the signed coordinate, carrying the value round each corner.
Evaluate ∮q<sub>b</sub> ds/t wall by wall and ∮ds/t, and find q<sub>s,0</sub>. Add it to every q<sub>b</sub>.
Take moments of q about a convenient point O: the moment equals S<sub>y</sub> times the distance from O to the shear centre.
Check that the vertical walls add up to S<sub>y</sub> and the horizontal walls to zero.

blocks.text: For a section symmetric about x, the shear centre lies on the x axis, and one load case (S<sub>y</sub>) gives its position along it. An unsymmetric section needs a second case with S<sub>x</sub> to find the other coordinate.

In a symmetric box under vertical shear, both vertical walls carry flow in the same physical direction, opposing the load. Read round the loop the two values have opposite signs, only because s runs up one wall and down the other. The shear centre of a doubly symmetric box with uniform walls is at the centroid.

Make one wall thicker and the symmetry about the vertical axis is lost. The thick wall is stiffer in shear, so in the zero-twist solution it takes a larger share of the shear force, and the resultant, which is the shear centre, moves towards it. A wing box with a heavy front spar web therefore has its shear centre ahead of mid-box. The shear centre does not follow the centroid, so each must be found by its own calculation.
If the real load acts elsewhere, the section carries the zero-twist flow plus a Bredt–Batho torsion flow T/2A, where T is the load times its offset from the shear centre.

figure.caption: The second worked example. Thickening the front wall to 4 mm makes it take 5.70 kN of the 10 kN shear in the zero-twist solution, so the shear centre S moves forward to 78.8 mm from the front wall, ahead of both the uniform-box position (100 mm) and the centroid G (85.7 mm).

Both vertical walls carry upward flow, 5.70 kilonewtons in the front wall and 4.30 in the rear wall. On the axis the shear centre S is at 78.8 millimetres from the front wall with the 10 kilonewton load on it, the centroid G at 85.7, and the uniform-box position at 100. A note says zero twist, the integral of q over t is zero, q nought is 63.64 newtons per millimetre, and the thick wall takes more shear.

examples.question: A rectangular box has mid-line width 200 mm, depth 100 mm and all walls 2 mm thick. It carries S<sub>y</sub> = 10 kN through its shear centre. Cut the left wall at mid-height and take s up the left wall, along the top, down the right wall and back along the bottom. Find q<sub>b</sub> at the corners, q<sub>s,0</sub>, and the final flows.
steps: Left wall, up from the cut: ∫t y ds = 2 × 50²/2 = 2500 mm³, so q<sub>b</sub> at the top-left corner = −0.00429 × 2500 = −10.71 N/mm.
Top wall (y = 50): adds 2 × 50 × 200 = 20,000 mm³. q<sub>b</sub> at the top-right corner = −96.43 N/mm.

Right wall: the upper half adds +2500 and the lower half −2500, so q<sub>b</sub> at the bottom-right corner is again −96.43 N/mm. Bottom wall (y = −50) removes 20,000: −10.71 N/mm at bottom-left, and the last half-wall brings q<sub>b</sub> back to 0 at the cut.

Uniform t, so q<sub>s,0</sub> = −(1/L)∮q<sub>b</sub> ds. Integrating each wall: ∮q<sub>b</sub> ds = −0.00429 × (2 × 41,667 + 2 × 2,500,000 + 2,416,667) = −32,143 N. L = 600 mm. q<sub>s,0</sub> = 53.57 N/mm.
Final flows: top-left and bottom-left corners 42.86 N/mm; top-right and bottom-right −42.86 N/mm; mid-height of the left wall 53.57, of the right wall −53.57 N/mm along s.

Read physically, both vertical walls carry flow upwards against the load; the top and bottom walls carry flows that reverse at mid-width. Moments confirm the shear centre at x = 100.0 mm, the mid-width, as symmetry requires.
examples.answer: q<sub>b</sub> = −10.71 and −96.43 N/mm at the corners; q<sub>s,0</sub> = 53.57 N/mm; final corner flows ±42.86 N/mm; shear centre at mid-width.

examples.question: The same box has its left (front) wall thickened to 4 mm; the other walls stay 2 mm. Find the shear centre.
steps: I<sub>xx</sub> = 4 × 100³/12 + 2 × 100³/12 + 2,000,000 = 2,500,000 mm⁴; S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub> = 0.0040 N/mm³. The cut and the path are as before.

q<sub>b</sub> in units of k = S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub>: left-upper wall −2s² (t = 4); top −(5000 + 100s); right −(25,000 + 100s − s²); bottom −(25,000 − 100s); left-lower −(5000 − 200s + 2s²), returning to 0 at the cut.

Wall forces ∫q ds along s: top 727.3 N, right wall −4,303.0 N (along s, downwards, so 4,303.0 N upwards), bottom 727.3 N, left wall 5,697.0 N upwards. Vertical check: 4,303.0 + 5,697.0 = 10,000 N = S<sub>y</sub>.
Moments about the left-wall mid-point O (the left wall passes through O): top and bottom forces act at 50 mm, the right wall at 200 mm. M<sub>O</sub> = 200 × 4,303.0 − 2 × 50 × 727.3 = 787,879 N·mm.

S<sub>y</sub> x<sub>s</sub> = M<sub>O</sub>, so x<sub>s</sub> = 787,879/10,000 = 78.8 mm from the front wall, 21.2 mm forward of mid-width. The centroid is at x̄ = 85.7 mm: the shear centre is ahead of it.
examples.answer: q<sub>s,0</sub> = 63.64 N/mm; the shear centre is 78.8 mm behind the front wall, against 100 mm for the uniform box; the centroid is at 85.7 mm.

traps: Stopping at q<sub>b</sub>. The open-section flow is not the answer for a closed section; add q<sub>s,0</sub>.
Saying q = 0 at the cut. The real flow at the cut is q<sub>s,0</sub>.
Using ∮q ds = 0 when the walls differ in thickness. The condition is ∮q ds/t = 0.
Taking the shear centre at the centroid of an unsymmetric box. In the second example they are 6.9 mm apart.
Mixing the signs of q<sub>b</sub> and q<sub>s,0</sub>. Both must be positive in the same direction of s.

quiz.q: What is q<sub>s,0</sub> in a closed-section shear calculation?
quiz.a: The constant shear flow at the imaginary cut, added all round the loop to the open-section flow q<sub>b</sub>.

quiz.q: Why can q<sub>s,0</sub> not be found from vertical and horizontal force equilibrium?
quiz.a: A constant flow round a closed loop has zero resultant force: the flows on opposite walls cancel. It has only a moment 2A q<sub>s,0</sub>, so it is found from a moment equation or from the twist condition.

quiz.q: A uniform-wall loop has ∮q<sub>b</sub> ds = −30,000 N and a perimeter of 600 mm. Find q<sub>s,0</sub>.
In the first example, what is the real shear flow at the cut?
Why does thickening the front wall move the shear centre forward?
quiz.a: Zero twist requires ∮q ds/t = 0. A thicker wall can carry more flow for the same strain, so the solution gives the front wall a larger share of the vertical shear (5.70 kN of 10 kN in the example). The resultant of the vertical flows moves towards it.

quiz.q: A load of 10 kN acts at mid-width of the thick-walled box. What extra flow does it cause?
quiz.a: The load is 21.2 mm behind the shear centre, so T = 10,000 × 21.2 = 212,121 N·mm. It adds a constant Bredt–Batho flow T/2A = 212,121/40,000 = 5.30 N/mm round the box.

beyond: Not for the exam. Shell finite element models of a wing box find the same flows without the cut; the cut method is still used to check them. Search for "shear centre of a closed section".
